categoryNote: Entries NX03-001..013. Boundary (TWEAK_CATALOGUE.md line 187): NX09 owns the power-PLAN lifecycle and the display/sleep/hibernate/fast-startup/lid/PCIe-ASPM/USB-suspend settings; NX03 owns the whole SUB_PROCESSOR subgroup 54533251-82be-4824-96c1-47b60b740d00 plus the three scheduler-adjacent machine knobs the catalogue assigns here (MMCSS SystemProfile, PriorityControl\Win32PrioritySeparation, PowerThrottling policy). NX09's Set-NxPlanSettingValue keeps its own hard rejection of the processor subgroup; NX03 has a separate engine for it and never weakens that guard. Every per-plan capture queries the AC and DC index SEPARATELY through NX09's shared fail-closed powercfg /query parser, journals both planes, writes only the requested planes and re-queries BOTH to verify. OVERRIDE-ABSENCE POLICY: powercfg /query reports only a plan's own overrides, and powercfg has no documented way to remove one, so a setting the plan does not carry is reported Skipped (no mutation) with the documented unhide + UI steps - NEXTRIX never journals an absence it could not restore byte-exactly. HIDDEN SETTINGS: Microsoft documents Boost mode, EPP, core parking and the performance policy family as hidden; value writes work regardless of UI visibility, and NEXTRIX documents the powercfg -attributes unhide command without ever flipping that machine-wide UI attribute itself. All GUIDs in this file were verified against the live PowerSettings store on 2026-11-23 and each setting's values/range against its Microsoft Learn page. No performance claims anywhere: configuration intent only, outcomes PENDING until owner evidence at E2+.

tweaks.name: Minimum processor state
tweaks.description: Sets the plan's minimum processor state (PROCTHROTTLEMIN) per AC and DC plane, with both original planes journaled for exact restore.
tweaks.objective: Give the owner explicit, plane-separated control of the documented lower bound of the processor performance range.
tweaks.technicalExplanation: Set-NxProcessorMinState targets SUB_PROCESSOR 54533251-82be-4824-96c1-47b60b740d00 :: PROCTHROTTLEMIN 893dee8e-2bef-41e0-89c6-b55d0929964c (alias confirmed by powercfg /aliases on this build), documented range 0..100 %. Microsoft defines the setting precisely as 'the minimum processor performance state, specified as a percentage of maximum processor performance' (and documents it as NOT hidden, unlike the boost/EPP/parking family). It is therefore the floor of the performance-state range that the processor power management engine will not go below when the platform honours the request. Both planes are captured separately through NX09's shared fail-closed powercfg /query parser and journaled in one original descriptor (acIndex/dcIndex as separate fields); only the requested planes are written via powercfg /setacvalueindex and /setdcvalueindex; verification re-queries and compares BOTH indexes; a failed verification restores both planes best-effort and journals the failure (safe stop). Rollback (Invoke-Nx03Rollback) is per-plane only-if-ours. LAPTOP CAUTION (P3 rule): a high AC minimum does not carry to battery behaviour because the DC plane is journaled and written independently - the emitted default keeps the AC floor at 100 % and the DC floor at 5 % so battery-specific behaviour is an explicit choice rather than a side effect. NEXTRIX makes no performance claim: the entry records configuration intent only, and the performance question stays PENDING until owner evidence. NOT WRITTEN BUT ADJACENT: boost mode (NX03-003) decides how far above nominal the processor may go, and maximum state (NX03-002) caps the top of the range; the three entries are independent settings and are never coupled implicitly.
tweaks.defaultState: Windows/OEM default: the plan's own minimum processor state values as shipped (commonly a low floor on battery planes; OEM images vary).
tweaks.proposedState: The chosen plan's minimum processor state equals the owner-selected AC and DC percentages, with both original planes journaled.

verify.procedure: powercfg /query re-read of PROCTHROTTLEMIN on the target plan returns the chosen AC and DC indexes; the journal verify entry records Verified with both planes (a skipped entry records the exact reason: no plan-level override present).

rollback.procedure: Invoke-Nx03Rollback -TweakId NX03-001 restores the journaled original AC and DC indexes per plane, only-if-ours: a plane changed by the owner after apply is reported diverged and left untouched.

originalState.method: Both the AC and DC index captured separately from powercfg /query BEFORE any change (fail-closed parse; absence of a plan-level override is itself a reported state and blocks the mutation) and journaled in the original descriptor.

sideEffects: A high minimum state keeps the processor out of low-power states on that plane: on battery this shortens runtime (stated as a preference, never as an improvement). The DC plane is independent and defaults to a low floor.
documentationSource: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows-hardware/customize/power-settings/options-for-perf-state-engine-minperformance (MinPerformance semantics; PowerCfg alias PROCTHROTTLEMIN; range 0..100 %; fetched 2026-11-23)
https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows-hardware/design/device-experiences/powercfg-command-line-options (setacvalueindex/setdcvalueindex/query; fetched 2026-11-23)

tweaks.name: Maximum processor state
tweaks.description: Sets the plan's maximum processor state (PROCTHROTTLEMAX) per AC and DC plane; the emitted default re-asserts the documented ceiling instead of capping it.
tweaks.objective: Explicit, plane-separated control of the documented upper bound of the performance range - including the ability to cap it deliberately - with exact rollback.
tweaks.technicalExplanation: Set-NxProcessorMaxState targets SUB_PROCESSOR :: PROCTHROTTLEMAX bc5038f7-23e0-4960-96da-33abaf5935ec (alias confirmed by powercfg /aliases), documented range 0..100 % and documented as NOT hidden. Microsoft defines it as 'the maximum processor performance state, specified as a percentage of maximum processor performance', i.e. the ceiling of the performance-state range: a value below 100 caps the whole range, which is the vendor-independent way to bound processor behaviour without touching firmware. BOOST INTERPLAY (documented, not inferred): Microsoft documents the boost mode (PERFBOOSTMODE, NX03-003) as deciding how processors select a performance level above the nominal level, so a maximum state below 100 bounds what boost may reach, while a 100 % maximum leaves boost policy as the only limiter. NEXTRIX never couples the two entries implicitly - each is journaled and rolled back on its own. The emitted default is 100/100 on both planes: a normalization action that restores the documented ceiling rather than an unrequested cap (a machine already at 100/100 records AlreadyAtState and changes nothing). Capping is an explicit owner parameter, and per the performance-claim policy this entry asserts no outcome in either direction. Capture/verify/restore are identical to NX03-001: both planes separately, fail-closed capture, re-query verification of both indexes, best-effort restore of both planes on a failed verify, per-plane only-if-ours rollback.
tweaks.defaultState: Windows/OEM default: maximum processor state normally 100 % on both planes (a cap, when present, was set by the OEM or the owner).
tweaks.proposedState: The chosen plan's maximum processor state equals the owner-selected AC and DC percentages (default action: the documented 100 % ceiling), with both original planes journaled.

verify.procedure: powercfg /query re-read of PROCTHROTTLEMAX returns the chosen AC and DC indexes; journal verify entry records Verified with both planes.

rollback.procedure: Invoke-Nx03Rollback -TweakId NX03-002 restores the journaled original AC and DC indexes per plane, only-if-ours.

originalState.method: Both the AC and DC index captured separately from powercfg /query before any change (fail-closed) and journaled; a missing plan-level override blocks the mutation and is reported with the unhide/UI steps.

sideEffects: A cap below 100 % deliberately lowers the performance ceiling on that plane (thermal/power intent); the emitted default does not cap. No cooling or performance outcome is claimed.
documentationSource: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows-hardware/customize/power-settings/options-for-perf-state-engine-maxperformance (MaxPerformance semantics; PowerCfg alias PROCTHROTTLEMAX; range 0..100 %; fetched 2026-11-23)
https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows-hardware/customize/power-settings/options-for-perf-state-engine-perfboostmode (documented boost/ceiling interplay; fetched 2026-11-23)

tweaks.name: Processor boost mode policy
tweaks.description: Sets the processor performance boost mode (PERFBOOSTMODE) per AC and DC plane, with the documented index meanings and vendor variance stated.
tweaks.objective: Let the owner choose a documented boost policy index per plane instead of relying on folklore values, with exact rollback.
tweaks.technicalExplanation: Set-NxProcessorBoostMode targets SUB_PROCESSOR :: PERFBOOSTMODE be337238-0d82-4146-a960-4f3749d470c7 (hidden setting). Microsoft's page documents the index table explicitly and it is NOT a single flat meaning: for ACPI P-State platforms 0=Disabled, 1=Enabled, 2=Enabled; for CPPC/PEP platforms 0=Disabled, 1=Enabled, 2=Aggressive (the OS selects a target boost performance when Enabled and the maximum boost performance when Aggressive); for autonomous CPPC/PEP the OS-side index does not override the platform decision. Indexes 3 and 4 exist as compatibility aliases of 1 and 2 in newer definitions. VENDOR SUPPORT VARIES, as the catalogue row states: whether the value changes observable behaviour depends on the platform type and the silicon vendor's implementation, and Microsoft's own processor-power-management guidance directs tuners to the silicon vendor before modifying these settings - NEXTRIX therefore journals the configuration, verifies the stored index, and claims nothing about the resulting frequency behaviour. HIDDEN SETTING: documented as hidden; NEXTRIX writes the plan value regardless of UI visibility (the flag is a machine-wide UI attribute outside the plan) and reports the documented powercfg -attributes SUB_PROCESSOR <guid> -ATTRIB_HIDE command instead of flipping that attribute itself. AC/DC discipline, fail-closed capture, re-query verification and per-plane rollback are identical to NX03-001; the emitted default is index 1 (documented 'Enabled') on both planes.
tweaks.defaultState: Windows/OEM default: boost policy as shipped by the platform/OEM profile (no plan-level override on most stock plans).
tweaks.proposedState: The chosen plan's boost mode index equals the owner-selected AC and DC indexes, with both original planes journaled.

verify.procedure: powercfg /query re-read of PERFBOOSTMODE returns the chosen AC and DC indexes; journal verify entry records Verified with both planes; a plan without the override returns Skipped with the documented unhide steps.

rollback.procedure: Invoke-Nx03Rollback -TweakId NX03-003 restores the journaled original AC and DC indexes per plane, only-if-ours.

originalState.method: Both the AC and DC index captured separately from powercfg /query before any change (fail-closed parse) and journaled; boot-time absence of the override is reported, never guessed.

sideEffects: Boost policy influences how far above nominal the platform may boost on platforms that honour the OS hint; thermal and power behaviour can change accordingly. No frequency or performance outcome is claimed (PENDING owner evidence).
documentationSource: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows-hardware/customize/power-settings/options-for-perf-state-engine-perfboostmode (GUID be337238-0d82-4146-a960-4f3749d470c7; alias PERFBOOSTMODE; index table per platform type; hidden setting; fetched 2026-11-23)
https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows-hardware/customize/power-settings/configure-processor-power-management-options (silicon-vendor tuning caution; fetched 2026-11-23)

tweaks.name: Energy Performance Preference
tweaks.description: Sets the processor energy performance preference (PERFEPP) per AC and DC plane, documenting where CPPC is a precondition and how AMD/Intel behaviour differs.
tweaks.objective: Give the owner the documented CPPC energy/performance hint per plane, with honest platform preconditions and exact rollback.
tweaks.technicalExplanation: Set-NxProcessorEnergyPreference targets SUB_PROCESSOR :: PERFEPP 36687f9e-e3a5-4dbf-b1dc-15eb381c6863 (hidden setting). Microsoft documents the semantics precisely: the value specifies what is programmed into the energy performance preference register on systems that implement version 2 of the CPPC interface AND have autonomous mode enabled; 0 programs the register to 0 (favour performance), 100 programs it to 255 (favour energy savings), and an intermediate value v is programmed as (v * 255) / 100. That is a precondition, not a guarantee: on platforms without CPPC v2 autonomous mode the setting is stored but drives nothing, and AMD vs Intel implementations of CPPC differ (AMD CPPC/P-state handoff versus Intel HWP/EPP semantics), so NEXTRIX reports the stored index and never claims an effect. The catalogue row records exactly this AMD/Intel behavioural difference. HIDDEN SETTING: documented as hidden; NEXTRIX writes the plan value regardless of UI visibility and reports the documented unhide command rather than flipping the machine-wide UI attribute. Emitted default 0 on AC and 100 on DC: an explicit, plane-separated choice (the P3 rule - AC and DC are never coupled) that is easy to reason about and easy to reverse; any other split is an owner parameter. AC/DC capture, re-query verification of both indexes, best-effort both-plane restore on failure and per-plane only-if-ours rollback are identical to NX03-001.
tweaks.defaultState: Windows/OEM default: EPP as configured by the platform profile (often no plan-level override; OEM tools may set one).
tweaks.proposedState: The chosen plan's EPP equals the owner-selected AC and DC percentages, with both original planes journaled.

verify.procedure: powercfg /query re-read of PERFEPP returns the chosen AC and DC indexes; journal verify entry records Verified with both planes. Verification is configuration-level only: whether the platform acts on the hint requires CPPC v2 + autonomous mode and is reported as a precondition, never asserted.

rollback.procedure: Invoke-Nx03Rollback -TweakId NX03-004 restores the journaled original AC and DC indexes per plane, only-if-ours.

originalState.method: Both the AC and DC index captured separately from powercfg /query before any change (fail-closed) and journaled; absence of a plan-level override blocks the mutation with the unhide/UI steps in the result.

sideEffects: Where CPPC v2 autonomous mode is active, the EPP hint shifts the platform's own frequency/energy trade-off on that plane; where it is not, the stored value has no effect. Stated as a precondition, not an outcome.
documentationSource: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows-hardware/customize/power-settings/options-for-perf-state-engine-perfenergypreference (GUID 36687f9e-e3a5-4dbf-b1dc-15eb381c6863; alias PERFEPP; CPPC v2 + autonomous-mode precondition; (setting*255)/100 mapping; hidden setting; fetched 2026-11-23)

https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows-hardware/customize/power-settings/configure-processor-power-management-options (heterogeneous/CPPC settings family context; silicon-vendor tuning caution; fetched 2026-11-23)

tweaks.name: Core parking policy
tweaks.description: Sets core parking minimum and/or maximum cores (CPMINCORES / CPMAXCORES) per AC and DC plane, documenting the hidden-setting unhide and the hardware dependence.
tweaks.objective: Let the owner bound how far the core-parking engine may park logical processors, with exact per-setting, per-plane rollback and the hidden-setting reality stated plainly.
tweaks.technicalExplanation: Set-NxCoreParkingPolicy targets two documented hidden settings: CPMINCORES 0cc5b647-c1df-4637-891a-dec35c318583 and CPMAXCORES ea062031-0e34-4ff1-9b6d-eb1059334028, both 0..100 % of the logical processors enabled within each NUMA node. Microsoft documents the minimum as the floor of the unparked set (25 % of 16 logical processors means at least 4 stay unparked) and states that a minimum of 100 % DISABLES the core-parking algorithm; the parking engine itself is described as the global scalability component of processor power management, which is why the effective unparked set remains hardware- and workload-dependent even after the value is set. The catalogue row flags exactly that hardware dependence and cross-references the NX19 scheduling profiles - NEXTRIX does not attempt to pick core counts here, it only bounds them. HIDDEN-SETTING UNHIDE (documented, never performed): Microsoft lists both settings as 'Hidden setting: Yes'. powercfg accepts the value writes regardless; UI visibility is a machine-wide attribute outside the plan, so NEXTRIX reports the documented command form (powercfg -attributes SUB_PROCESSOR <guid> -ATTRIB_HIDE, plus the +ATTRIB_HIDE reverse) and never flips that attribute itself. TRANSACTION SHAPE: the two settings are separate engine calls with separate AC/DC captures; a failure on CPMINCORES stops the CPMaxCORES step so the pair is never half-configured, and an inverted min>max pair is rejected before any mutation. Emitted default touches only the AC plane (acMinCores 100, the documented 'parking disabled' bound) so battery behaviour is never changed by a performance-intent action; owners parameterize the rest.
tweaks.defaultState: Windows/OEM default: parking bounds as shipped by the platform profile; both settings hidden in the UI and often absent as plan-level overrides.
tweaks.proposedState: The chosen plan's parking minimum and/or maximum equals the owner-selected per-plane percentages, each setting journaled with both original planes.

verify.procedure: powercfg /query re-read of CPMINCORES (and CPMAXCORES when supplied) returns the chosen AC and DC indexes; each engine call journals its own verify entry. A missing plan-level override returns Skipped with the documented unhide command in the result.

rollback.procedure: Invoke-Nx03Rollback -TweakId NX03-005 restores each setting's journaled original AC and DC indexes in reverse order, only-if-ours; the two settings are independent entries so one can be restored without the other.

originalState.method: For each of the two settings: both the AC and DC index captured separately from powercfg /query before any change (fail-closed) and journaled in that setting's original descriptor.

sideEffects: Parking bounds change which logical processors the OS keeps available: a raised minimum keeps more cores unparked on that plane (power/thermal cost) while a lowered maximum allows more aggressive parking. Effective behaviour stays platform-dependent - no outcome is claimed.
documentationSource: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows-hardware/customize/power-settings/options-for-core-parking-cpmincores (CPMinCores semantics; 100 % disables parking; PowerCfg CPMINCORES; 0..100 %; hidden setting; fetched 2026-11-23)
https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows-hardware/customize/power-settings/options-for-core-parking-cpmaxcores (CPMaxCores; PowerCfg CPMAXCORES; 0..100 %; hidden setting; fetched 2026-11-23)

https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows-hardware/customize/power-settings/configure-processor-power-management-options (core parking engine described as the global scalability component; fetched 2026-11-23)

tweaks.name: CPU power throttling policy
tweaks.description: Switches the machine-wide PowerThrottling (EcoQoS) policy value, with the documented mechanism and the value-name provenance recorded honestly.
tweaks.objective: Let the owner decide explicitly whether Windows may lower the QoS class of background work, with exact rollback of the exact original value.
tweaks.technicalExplanation: Set-NxPowerThrottlingPolicy writes HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Power\PowerThrottling :: PowerThrottlingOff as a DWord: 1 disables power throttling, 0 restores Windows' default behaviour. HONEST PROVENANCE SPLIT: Microsoft documents the PowerThrottling key and the QoS/EcoQoS mechanism in the quality-of-service page (Windows classifies work into QoS levels, lowers the QoS policy of some background/user-inactive work, and lets an application opt out), but the documentation does not describe this specific value name - so the entry is CONDITIONAL, the value-name provenance is labelled community-established (E0 for the name, E1 for the mechanism), and the trade-off is stated instead of a benefit: disabling removes the OS lever that lowers background work's QoS class, which changes power/thermal behaviour on battery-first machines and interacts with the OS scheduling hints that hybrid (P/E) platforms use. Because the mechanism is machine-wide and the value can be ABSENT on a stock install, the transaction engine journals the exact registry descriptor (key existence, value existence, kind, data) and the shared rollback engine restores it byte-exactly or deletes the value if it never existed. Profiles exclude P3 (battery-first) and the entry is never preset-applied; POWER-THROTTLING IS NOT A PERFORMANCE CLAIM - NEXTRIX records which policy is in force, not what it buys.
tweaks.defaultState: Windows default: power throttling active (PowerThrottlingOff absent or 0 depending on the image).
tweaks.proposedState: PowerThrottlingOff holds the owner-selected DWord (1 = throttling disabled, 0 = default behaviour) with the exact original descriptor journaled.

verify.procedure: Test-NxConfigurationState read-back of PowerThrottlingOff equals the chosen DWord; journal verify entry records Verified. The result carries the provenance split and the hybrid-interaction note.

rollback.procedure: Invoke-NxRollback -TweakId NX03-006 restores the exact original via the shared registry engine: value rewritten with its original kind, or deleted when it never existed (only-if-ours first - divergence reported, never clobbered).

originalState.method: Capture-NxRegistryValue records key existence, value existence, kind and exact data for PowerThrottlingOff before any write; the whole value set is captured before the first write.

sideEffects: Removes the OS's documented QoS-lowering lever machine-wide: background work keeps its QoS class, which costs power/thermal budget on battery-first machines and can alter hybrid scheduling behaviour. Never offered to P3.
If the PowerThrottling key does not exist yet it is created; rollback restores/deletes the value exactly but leaves the (empty) key in place - an additive shell, documented rather than hidden.
documentationSource: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/procthread/quality-of-service (documents the PowerThrottling key and the QoS/EcoQoS mechanism, including DisableUserPresenceQos; fetched 2026-11-23)

tweaks.name: MMCSS configuration
tweaks.description: Configures the documented MMCSS surface: SystemResponsiveness and, opt-in, per-task Priority / Scheduling Category for existing MMCSS tasks.
tweaks.objective: Give the owner the documented MMCSS knobs with exact per-value rollback, and leave the undocumented/unused ones untouched.
tweaks.technicalExplanation: Set-NxMmcssConfiguration writes only what Microsoft documents for the Multimedia Class Scheduler Service: HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion\Multimedia\SystemProfile :: SystemResponsiveness (REG_DWORD percentage of CPU reserved for low-priority work - values not divisible by 10 round down, values below 10 or above 100 are clamped to 20, and 100 disables MMCSS entirely, the driver returning STATUS_SERVER_DISABLED) plus, opt-in, SystemProfile\Tasks\<task> :: Priority (REG_DWORD 1..8; for a task whose Scheduling Category is High the value is always treated as 2) and Scheduling Category (REG_SZ High|Medium|Low) for EXISTING task keys. The MMCSS SERVICE itself is never reconfigured here: service start types belong to NX11 (Background & Services), and disabling MMCSS would make every value in this entry meaningless - so NEXTRIX configures the documented policy surface and leaves service state alone. DELIBERATELY NOT WRITTEN: GPU Priority and SFIO Priority (Microsoft documents both as unused), Clock Rate (the guarantee was removed in Windows 7), Affinity and BackgroundPriority (not needed by any NEXTRIX objective and each changes scheduling in ways the owner did not ask for). No task keys are invented. TRANSACTION: every requested value is captured first and written through the NX03 all-or-nothing engine - a failure restores every already-written value in reverse order to its exact original before the failure is journaled. STOCK-STATE HONESTY (research: stock SystemResponsiveness is 20; the reference ecosystem writes 10 with no evidence of benefit): the emitted default writes 10 because that is the owner-visible intent of the classic MMCSS tweak, but the entry is ADVANCED, preset-excluded, records the stock value on the way in, and asserts no outcome. SCOPE/XREF: this is the machine-wide MMCSS policy; NX17-008 (system responsiveness value) and NX17-010 (multimedia scheduler configuration) are XREF entries that delegate here so there is exactly one write path and no duplicate targets.
tweaks.defaultState: Windows default: SystemResponsiveness 20 and the stock task table (Audio/Capture/Distribution/Games/Playback/Pro Audio/Window Manager) with OEM additions.
tweaks.proposedState: SystemResponsiveness and/or the selected existing task's Priority/Scheduling Category hold the owner-selected values, with every original descriptor journaled individually.

verify.procedure: Test-NxConfigurationState read-back of each written value (SystemResponsiveness, and per-task Priority / Scheduling Category when supplied) equals the chosen data; each value has its own journal verify entry; the result reports the MMCSS-disabled note when 100 is chosen.

rollback.procedure: Invoke-NxRollback -TweakId NX03-007 restores every journaled value to its exact original (kind + data, or deletion when it never existed), newest first, only-if-ours.

originalState.method: Capture-NxRegistryValue per value (key existence, value existence, kind, data) before the first write; the whole set is validated and captured before mutation.

sideEffects: MMCSS reserves CPU for low-priority work: lowering SystemResponsiveness reserves less, which changes how multimedia-tagged and background work compete machine-wide. Per-task values change the priority band a participating task receives. Configuration intent only - no latency or frame-time claim.
documentationSource: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/procthread/multimedia-class-scheduler-service (SystemResponsiveness semantics/clamping/100-disables; task value table incl. Priority 1..8, Scheduling Category High|Medium|Low, GPU/SFIO Priority documented as unused; fetched 2026-11-23)

tweaks.name: Win32PrioritySeparation
tweaks.description: Writes PriorityControl\Win32PrioritySeparation with an owner-supplied value, documenting exactly what Microsoft does and does not document - and why NEXTRIX picks no 'optimized' value.
tweaks.objective: Make the one documented scheduler value controllable with exact rollback while refusing to launder folklore into configuration.
tweaks.technicalExplanation: Set-NxWin32PrioritySeparation writes HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\PriorityControl :: Win32PrioritySeparation as a DWord. WHAT MICROSOFT DOCUMENTS: the Win32_OperatingSystem class maps its ForegroundApplicationBoost property to 'Win32Registry|SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\PriorityControl|Win32PrioritySeparation' and documents the boost levels - None (0), Minimum (1), Maximum (2) - as implemented by boosting the foreground quantum by 6, 12 and 18 respectively; the class default is reported as 2. WHAT MICROSOFT DOES NOT DOCUMENT: the six-bit field encoding (short vs long quantum, variable vs fixed, boost ratio) that community guides quote, and therefore what 36, 38, 42, 0x2A or 26 actually mean. THE DIVERGENCE IS THE FINDING: five reference projects ship five different values - 36 (Vain, SynergyOS), 38 (XOS, ReviOS), 42/0x2A (SapphireOS), 26 with a picker UI (SynergyOS SOS folder) - with zero published evidence (docs/RESEARCH_RECONCILIATION.md catalogue change queue item 4). CONSEQUENCE FOR THE ENGINE: the function requires an explicit value 0..63 (the documented field width), never picks an 'optimized' one, and the emitted default re-asserts the documented class default 2 - a normalization action, not a tuning action. The returned interpretation separates the documented boost-level mapping from an explicitly UNdocumented bit-field reading, records the reference divergence, and marks the performance question PENDING. It is also a GLOBAL knob: the foreground/background quantum policy cannot be scoped, and ReviOS's revert.yml (r2) is the standing ledger of global scheduler/service changes that broke real software - hence preset-excluded plus ExplicitConsent. The registry transaction journals the exact descriptor (including absence and kind) and the shared rollback engine restores it byte-exactly.
tweaks.defaultState: Windows default: Win32PrioritySeparation as shipped (commonly 2 on client SKUs; OEM/reference tools frequently leave 36/38/42 behind).
tweaks.proposedState: Win32PrioritySeparation holds the owner-supplied DWord with the exact original descriptor journaled and the documented/undocumented split reported back.

verify.procedure: Test-NxConfigurationState read-back of Win32PrioritySeparation equals the supplied DWord; the journal verify entry records Verified; the result's interpretation object states the documented boost level (or that the value is outside it) and labels the bit-field reading undocumented.

rollback.procedure: Invoke-NxRollback -TweakId NX03-008 restores the exact original via the shared registry engine (original kind and data, or deletion when the value never existed), only-if-ours.

originalState.method: Capture-NxRegistryValue records key existence, value existence, kind and exact data before the write; Get-NxWin32PrioritySeparationReport provides the same reading read-only for planning.

sideEffects: Foreground/background quantum policy is global: every process competes under it, and reference projects disagree on the value by a factor of the whole field. No performance outcome is claimed in either direction; the owner-visible effect is the documented boost level.
documentationSource: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/cimwin32prov/win32-operatingsystem (ForegroundApplicationBoost MappingStrings to PriorityControl\Win32PrioritySeparation; None/Minimum/Maximum boost levels with 6/12/18 quantum boosts; class default 2; fetched 2026-11-23)

tweaks.name: Processor performance policy set
tweaks.description: Sets the documented processor performance threshold/hysteresis/policy settings per plane, and refuses the time-check interval whose units Microsoft never documents.
tweaks.objective: Expose the documented performance-policy family with per-setting, per-plane rollback - and demonstrate what NEXTRIX will not write when documentation is missing.
tweaks.technicalExplanation: Set-NxProcessorPerformancePolicy targets six documented hidden settings, each with a Microsoft page stating values, units and range: PERFINCTHRESHOLD 06cadf0e-64ed-448a-8927-ce7bf90eb35d and PERFDECTHRESHOLD 12a0ab44-fe28-4fa9-b3bd-4b64f44960a6 (0..100 %, the utilisation band that triggers a performance-state change), PERFINCTIME 984cf492-3bed-4488-a8f9-4286c97bf5aa and PERFDECTIME d8edeb9b-95cf-4f95-a73c-b061973693c8 (0..100 TIME CHECK INTERVALS - not microseconds and not percentages, which is exactly where folklore goes wrong), PERFINCPOL 465e1f50-b610-473a-ab58-00d1077dc418 (0..3: ideal state / one step closer to ideal / highest state / ideal optimized for responsiveness) and PERFDECPOL 40fbefc7-2e9d-4d25-a185-0cfd8574bac6 (0..2: ideal / one step closer to ideal / lowest state). Microsoft documents the family as applying to systems where the OS drives non-autonomous performance states, i.e. behaviour on autonomous-CPPC platforms is platform-decided - stated as a precondition, never an outcome. WHAT IS DELIBERATELY NOT EXPOSED: the processor performance time check interval (4d2b0152-7d5c-498b-88e2-34345392a2c5, GUID live-verified in this build's PowerSettings store). Microsoft publishes no unit/range page for it, so every reference sets it by folklore; exposing an unverified unit invites wrong magnitudes, and the function returns this exclusion explicitly so the gap is documented rather than hidden. TRANSACTION SHAPE: each requested setting is a separate engine call with its own AC/DC capture and verify; a failure stops the remaining settings (every applied step stays journaled and restorable) and the emitted default writes only the two documented policy indexes at index 0 (documented 'select the ideal processor performance state') on both planes - a baseline normalization, not a tuning claim.
tweaks.defaultState: Windows/OEM default: the plan's own thresholds, hysteresis times and policy indexes (often no plan-level overrides; hidden in the UI).
tweaks.proposedState: Each requested setting equals the owner-selected per-plane index, journaled per setting with both original planes.

verify.procedure: powercfg /query re-read of each written setting returns the chosen AC and DC indexes; each setting has its own journal verify entry; settings the plan does not override return Skipped with the unhide steps, and the excluded time-check interval is always reported in the result.

rollback.procedure: Invoke-Nx03Rollback -TweakId NX03-009 restores each setting's journaled original AC and DC indexes (reverse journal order), only-if-ours; settings are independent so any subset can be restored.

originalState.method: Per setting: both the AC and DC index captured separately from powercfg /query before any change (fail-closed) and journaled in that setting's original descriptor.

sideEffects: Thresholds and hysteresis times change how eagerly the OS moves between performance states on non-autonomous platforms, which affects power/thermal behaviour and responsiveness characteristics. No metric is claimed; the time-check interval is not exposed at all.
documentationSource: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows-hardware/customize/power-settings/options-for-perf-state-engine-perfincreasethreshold (0..100 %; alias PERFINCTHRESHOLD; hidden; fetched 2026-11-23)

https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows-hardware/customize/power-settings/options-for-perf-state-engine-perfincreasetime (units = time check intervals; 0..100; hidden; fetched 2026-11-23)

tweaks.name: SMT / Hyper-Threading configuration
tweaks.description: Read-only SMT/topology report plus guided firmware steps. SMT is a firmware setting; NEXTRIX implements no OS-level toggle and says so.
tweaks.objective: Tell the owner the observed SMT state and exactly where the change really lives, instead of shipping a fake 'disable SMT' write.
tweaks.technicalExplanation: Get-NxSmtTopologyReport reports, strictly read-only, what the OS can observe: per-socket physical core and logical processor counts from Win32_Processor (NumberOfCores / NumberOfLogicalProcessors), the derived SMT inference (logical > physical => appears active), and the hypervisor flag - because a hypervisor can expose arbitrary counts, the inference is explicitly marked Uncertain in that case. The configuration itself is NOT implemented and cannot be: Windows exposes no supported OS-level SMT/Hyper-Threading switch; enablement lives in UEFI/BIOS (Intel: Hyper-Threading / Hyper-Threading Technology; AMD: SMT Mode / Simultaneous Multithreading, with per-board wording differences) and the OS simply schedules on the logical processors firmware reports. The entry therefore remains status Defined with modificationType none: the deliverable is the report plus guided steps (confirm the firmware option name, change it in firmware, re-check NX03-013 and any NX19 topology-based selection afterwards, expect per-core licensed software and virtual machines to react differently). HIGH BLAST RADIUS is the reason the catalogue marks it ADVANCED and preset-excluded: disabling SMT halves the logical processor count available to every workload, and NEXTRIX will not take that decision on the owner's behalf. Deep P/E or die-level topology is deliberately NOT derived here - EfficiencyClass tiers and CCD/X3D detection belong to the NX19 topology engine, and this report never guesses them from marketing names.
tweaks.defaultState: Not applicable - firmware-owned state; nothing is written by this entry.
tweaks.proposedState: A read-only topology report with an explicitly uncertain-aware SMT inference and guided firmware steps; no configuration is changed.

verify.procedure: Report returns readOnly=true, noWritesPerformed=true, per-socket counts, smtState (or Uncertain with the reason) and osLevelToggleAvailable=false with the documented rationale.

rollback.procedure: Not applicable - read-only report; an actual SMT change is made in firmware by the owner and is outside NEXTRIX's mutation surface.

originalState.method: Not applicable - no configuration change. The report records the observed topology as context only.

sideEffects: None (read-only CIM/WMI queries). The guided firmware change the owner performs is outside NEXTRIX and changes the logical processor count system-wide.
documentationSource: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/cimwin32prov/win32-processor (NumberOfCores / NumberOfLogicalProcessors / MaxClockSpeed fields; fetched 2026-11-23)

https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/api/sysinfoapi/nf-sysinfoapi-getlogicalprocessorinformationex (the documented topology interface the NX19 engine uses for EfficiencyClass tiers - referenced, not re-implemented here; fetched 2026-11-23)

tweaks.name: AMD CPPC preferred cores
tweaks.description: Read-only AMD-platform report for CPPC/preferred-core reality: no documented OS control interface exists, so nothing is written and the state is Unknown.
tweaks.objective: Replace an unimplementable 'preferred cores' tweak with an honest platform report and a vendor gate that actually checks the CPU.
tweaks.technicalExplanation: Get-NxAmdPreferredCoreReport detects the CPU vendor from Win32_Processor.Manufacturer (never from a name list) and reports platform applicability INSIDE the function. This is deliberate: NxCompat exposes no CPU-vendor gate, and using requiredHardware.gpuVendor for a CPU decision would gate on the wrong component - so requiredHardware stays empty and the honest gate lives in code, with platformAvailable/platformReason in the result. WHAT IS REAL: on AMD platforms that implement CPPC, Windows drives the energy-performance preference register through the documented PERFEPP setting and the autonomous-mode setting; both are READ here (override presence and both planes) and neither is written by this entry - EPP configuration, when the owner wants it, belongs to NX03-004. WHAT IS NOT REAL: there is no Microsoft- or vendor-documented OS interface to select or pin preferred cores; the ranking is firmware/CCPC-managed, so preferredCoreControl='NotDocumented' and preferredCoreState='Unknown' rather than a fabricated value. X3D/CCD INTERPLAY (research r1/r3): the reliable signal on dual-CCD X3D parts is per-die L3 asymmetry, not a marketing-name list - that detection is the NX19 topology engine's job and this report marks it Uncertain instead of guessing. EVIDENCE: E0 by design; the catalogue class is EXPERIMENTAL and the entry is never preset-offered. Status Defined: the report ships, the configuration does not exist and is not pretended to.
tweaks.defaultState: Not applicable - platform/firmware-managed; nothing is written by this entry.
tweaks.proposedState: A read-only AMD-platform report: vendor gate result, read-only CPPC setting snapshot, preferredCoreState=Unknown with the documentation-absence reason, no firmware writes.

verify.procedure: Report returns readOnly=true, noWritesPerformed=true, cpuVendor from CIM, platformAvailable consistent with the vendor, preferredCoreControl=NotDocumented, preferredCoreState=Unknown and the provenance/uncertainty lists populated.

rollback.procedure: Not applicable - read-only report; no configuration is changed and no firmware is touched.

originalState.method: Not applicable - no change. Only read-only CPPC setting snapshots are included as context.

sideEffects: None (read-only). NEXTRIX never writes firmware or vendor driver state for this entry.
documentationSource: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows-hardware/customize/power-settings/options-for-perf-state-engine-perfenergypreference (the documented CPPC-v2/autonomous-mode EPP surface that IS readable; fetched 2026-11-23)
research/sources/r1-fsosx-xos.md (X3D/CCD0 die heuristics are vendor-described and unverified; L3 asymmetry, not name lists, is the reliable signal)
research/sources/r3-sapphire-vain.md (scheduler/'best cores' engines are closed and unverifiable - the anti-pattern this entry refuses to copy)

tweaks.name: Intel hybrid P/E power policy
tweaks.description: Read-only Intel-platform report for the heterogeneous policy settings family; hybrid topology stays Uncertain until the NX19 topology engine exists, and nothing is written.
tweaks.objective: Report what is genuinely observable on an Intel hybrid platform without inventing a P/E policy NEXTRIX cannot document or verify.
tweaks.technicalExplanation: Get-NxIntelHybridPolicyReport detects the CPU vendor from Win32_Processor.Manufacturer and gates applicability inside the function (same reasoning as NX03-011: NxCompat has no CPU-vendor gate and gpuVendor would gate the wrong component, so requiredHardware stays empty and the gate is explicit in code). It then reads, strictly read-only, the documented heterogeneous settings family in SUB_PROCESSOR - heterogeneous policy in effect (7f2f5cfa-f10c-4823-b5e1-e93ae85f46b5), heterogeneous thread scheduling policy (93b8b6dc-0698-4d1c-9ee4-0644e900c85d) and heterogeneous short running thread scheduling policy (bae08b81-2d5e-4688-ad6a-13243356654b), all GUIDs live-verified in the PowerSettings store - reporting override presence and both planes. HYBRID TOPOLOGY IS NOT GUESSED: P/E classification requires EfficiencyClass tiers from GetLogicalProcessorInformationEx(RelationProcessorCore), which the NX19 topology engine owns, so hybridTopology='Uncertain-HybridTopologyRequiresNX19Engine' and the report says so rather than inferring from processor names (research r1 shows name-list approaches misclassify). DOCUMENTED SCOPE: Microsoft documents the processor power management settings family, including the Hetero*/efficiency-class variants, as an OEM/silicon-vendor tuning surface and explicitly directs tuners to the silicon vendor before modifying them; there is no end-user P/E policy contract. NEXTRIX therefore writes nothing here: the deliverable is the report, the documented-scope statement, and the guidance (leave P/E placement to Windows plus current firmware/chipset drivers; Game Mode is the documented OS-level lever during play and is NX02-001's, not a P/E policy). EVIDENCE: E0 by design; catalogue class EXPERIMENTAL; never preset-offered. Status Defined: the report ships, the configuration is intentionally absent.
tweaks.defaultState: Not applicable - platform/OS-managed; nothing is written by this entry.
tweaks.proposedState: A read-only Intel-platform report: vendor gate result, read-only heterogeneous-policy setting snapshot, hybridTopology=Uncertain with the reason, no writes anywhere.

verify.procedure: Report returns readOnly=true, noWritesPerformed=true, cpuVendor from CIM, platformAvailable consistent with the vendor, hybridTopology marked Uncertain with its reason, heterogeneous policy settings listed read-only, and the documented-scope/guidance text present.

rollback.procedure: Not applicable - read-only report; no configuration is changed.

originalState.method: Not applicable - no change. The report records current heterogeneous-policy values as context only.

sideEffects: None (read-only). NEXTRIX never writes the heterogeneous policy settings on the owner's behalf.
documentationSource: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows-hardware/customize/power-settings/configure-processor-power-management-options (heterogeneous settings family, efficiency-class variants, and the explicit 'reach out to your silicon vendor' caution; fetched 2026-11-23)
research/sources/r1-fsosx-xos.md (P/E detection requires GetLogicalProcessorInformationEx EfficiencyClass tiers; name-list heuristics are unreliable)

tweaks.name: CPU inventory & frequency report
tweaks.description: Read-only CPU inventory: sockets, cores, threads, firmware-reported frequencies, caches, virtualization flags, and which processor power settings the active plan actually overrides.
tweaks.objective: One evidence base for CPU decisions - and the precondition report that tells the owner which NX03 mutations can actually apply on this plan.
tweaks.technicalExplanation: Get-NxCpuInventoryReport extends (never replaces) NxHardware's Get-NxCpuReport: when that helper is loaded its vendor/name/core classification is reused so the two reports cannot disagree, and the CIM read adds per-socket detail - name, manufacturer, socket designation, address width, NumberOfCores / NumberOfLogicalProcessors, MaxClockSpeed and CurrentClockSpeed, L2/L3 cache sizes, VirtualizationFirmwareEnabled, VMMonitorModeExtensions, SecondLevelAddressTranslationExtensions and Status. FREQUENCY HONESTY: MaxClockSpeed and CurrentClockSpeed are firmware-reported CIM fields (nominal and last-reported), not measurements - NEXTRIX takes no sample, computes no average and makes no frequency claim; the report states this in a frequencyNote field. It also reads the hypervisor flag, because a hypervisor changes what core counts mean. The second half is the operationally important one: for each of the twelve NX03-owned processor settings it reports whether the ACTIVE plan carries a plan-level override plus the AC and DC indexes, read-only through NX09's shared parser. That is exactly the precondition the per-plan engine enforces - powercfg reports only a plan's own overrides and cannot restore an absence - so this report is how an owner sees in advance which of NX03-001..009 will apply and which will return Skipped with the unhide steps. Any unreadable read is an Uncertainty entry, never a guessed value (SynToolkit pattern, r4).
tweaks.proposedState: A machine-readable + human-readable CPU inventory with the active plan's processor-setting override snapshot; nothing is changed.

verify.procedure: Report returns readOnly=true, noWritesPerformed=true, readSucceeded=true with at least one socket entry, totals populated or explicitly null with an uncertainty entry, and the per-setting override snapshot covering all twelve NX03 settings (or processorSettingsAvailable=false with the reason).

sideEffects: None beyond a brief CIM query and a dozen read-only powercfg /query calls; on configurations where powercfg /query needs elevation the affected rows are reported as unmatched/uncertain instead of guessed.
documentationSource: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/cimwin32prov/win32-processor (inventory fields incl. NumberOfCores, NumberOfLogicalProcessors, MaxClockSpeed, CurrentClockSpeed, cache sizes, virtualization flags; fetched 2026-11-23)
https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows-hardware/design/device-experiences/powercfg-command-line-options (read-only /query the override snapshot relies on; fetched 2026-11-23)
